work.title: Passion of Artemon, priest of Laodicea (24 March)

paragraphs.text: March 24. The passion of the holy priest and martyr Artemius. In the twenty-fourth year of Emperor Diocletian's reign, a great disturbance arose, and there was an investigation into demons and idols. He sent an edict to every city and throughout the whole land, ordering an inspection of all the shrines, especially those adorned with costly gold. A certain count arrived in the region of Laodicea, and, entering the city, he inspected the temple sites. There stood a shrine of Apollo, and, finding a sacrifice, he offered incense to them. But Bishop Sisinnius, together with the priest Artemon, entered the temple of Artemis, smashed all the idols, and burned them with fire. When the Christians who were in the city heard this, they gathered in the church of God. Bishop Sisinnius taught them, saying

to Christ's servants, “My children, has any of you separated himself from the love of Christ? For the Antichrist has entered the city; he will destroy the Christians.” That day the count held games, spectacles, and hunts, continuing for another five days. Then he entered the temple of Artemis and inspected the temple's idols. Some of the pagans accused the bishop, saying that Bishop Sisinnius, together with the priest Artemon, had smashed the idols of Artemis. When the count heard that all these Christians had gathered in the church together with the bishop, he ordered his soldiers to saddle an imperial horse for him, so that he could enter the church in his armor, shed the Christians' blood, and seize Bishop Sisinnius together with the priest Artemon. He went out of the city with his soldiers, for the church was five stadia from the city. As he approached the church, when he was about one stadion away, he began to shake, and a great fire began to burn him, so that he fell from his horse and lay dying. They brought a stretcher, laid him on it, and carried him into the praetorium. When midnight

came, the count ordered lamps to be brought and lit throughout the praetorium, and his soldiers to remain with him. He said to his attendants, “Surely the Christians have cursed me, and their God is tormenting me.” His attendants said to him, “The revered gods and the holiness of the goddess Artemis will protect you.” But as he was suffering terribly and could not endure the pain, he ordered his soldiers to go to the church. and tell Bishop Sisinnius, “The God of the Christians is great. Pray to God for me, so that I may rise and escape this torment, and I will set up a golden image of you in this city.” The soldiers went and told the bishop what they had heard. The bishop answered them, “Go and tell your count: ‘May your gold and your silver remain with you. But if you believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, you will escape that terrible illness.’” He replied, “I believe, if only I may escape this.” Immediately he became well. He ordered his soldiers to harness a carriage for them, so that he could go with them to the city of Caesarea.

When he had left the city of Laodicea and traveled three stadia, Artemon, the servant of God, met him, returning from a hunt, having caught wild animals by the word of Christ. Two deer and six wild goats followed behind him. They were going to Bishop Sisinnius. For Bishop Sisinnius had a beautiful garden. The count ordered the carriage to stop and questioned Artemon, the servant of God, about how he had caught these animals. For the count thought that they were hand-reared and tame. Artemon, the servant of God, said to him, “They were caught by the word of Christ.” The count said, “Old man, am I to understand, then, that you are a Christian?” Artemon said, “I have been a Christian since childhood.” The count immediately ordered that chains be put around his neck, that he be handed over to two soldiers, and that he follow him all the way to the city of Caesarea. Then Saint Artemon commanded the deer and the wild goats to go to the bishop’s garden. They hurried away and stood near the city. When the bishop saw them,

he said to the gatekeeper, “Where have these wild goats and deer come from?” Immediately one of the deer opened its mouth and said in a human voice, “Artemon, the servant of God, has been seized by the impious count. As he was going to the city of Caesarea, he was bound and handed over to two soldiers. He commanded us to come to this garden.” The bishop was astonished at the deer’s human voice, and, not believing the report about Saint Artemon, he ordered the gatekeeper to summon Phileas the deacon. When he came, the bishop said to him, “Phileas the deacon, do you see these wild goats and deer standing near the city?” The deacon said to him, “Yes, my lord, I see them.” I have a wondrous miracle to tell you about, Phileas. For one of the deer spoke with a human voice, saying that the priest and servant of God Artemon had been seized by the impious count and was going to Caesarea. And terror seizes me at the deer's human voice. And if this is so, come and receive a blessing, and go to Caesarea with one servant, and find out whether this is

true. For there is great sorrow within me. The deacon received a blessing from the bishop, prayed, and went on his way. When he reached Caesarea, he searched for Artemon, the servant of the Lord. The holy man was in prison. The deacon found him and said to him, “Servant of God Most High and shepherd of rational sheep, how have you left us alone and fallen into the hands of the tormentors, without any of us knowing? Only one of the wild animals told the bishop that Artemon, the servant of God, had been seized by the impious count and was going to Caesarea. The bishop did not believe it, and so he sent me here to find out whether what he had heard was true. For he is deeply troubled about you.” Saint Artemon said to him, “Phileas, servant of God, go and tell my master, the holy bishop, to pray for me, so that I may defeat the impious and Christ-hating schemer and become a partaker in Christ. For I have not yet been questioned. Go, then, and tell the bishop that Artemon, the servant of God, is confined in prison and asks that you pray for him.” The bishop prayed, saying,

“Lord Jesus Christ, who delivered Daniel from the mouths of lions, who delivered the three young men from the fire of the furnace of King Nebuchadnezzar, deliver your servant Artemon also from the tormentor, the count, and grant him victory over all the schemes that he devises against him.” After the count had held the customary public spectacles, he ordered Artemon, the servant of God, to be brought before him the next day. When he arrived, the count said to him, “Tell me, old man, what is your name?” He replied, “Artemon.” The count said, “Are you the one who destroyed and shattered the great goddess Artemis?” Saint Artemon said, “I am.” The count said, “Tell me, old man, how did you scorn her power, and yet she did not become angry with you? [?] I tell you, because she is merciful, she has therefore granted you life and has not killed you.” Saint Artemon said, “I will put you to shame by praying to my God, so that I may overcome your tyranny. And can I not put that dead and mute idol to shame?” The count said, “You were rightly named Artemon. For, as I think, you are a servant of the goddess Artemis, and because you bear her name, for that reason

she has given you life.” Saint Artemon said, “You unclean and ungodly son of the devil, darkened in mind! If you wish to learn about my name, then know that while I was still in my mother’s womb, my name was given to me through a vow.” The count said, “Honor your old age and show respect for your gray hair, and sacrifice to the great god Asclepius.” The martyr said, “I spent sixteen years as a reader, reading the divine books. And I spent twenty-eight years reading Christ’s Gospel. And I spent three years as a priest, teaching the power of God, and I did not sacrifice to idols. And now do you command me to sacrifice to a senseless demon like yourself? If, then, you wish me to sacrifice to him, let us both go into the temple where your god stands, and I will sacrifice to him.” The count said, “But the great god Asclepius has his own glory. And unless he receives an offering of incense and sacrifices, you cannot enter the temple.” Now there were serpents living in that temple, and once a year the priests gave sweet food

to them. The saint said, “Let us go into the temple. If he does not receive me or allow me to enter the temple, then I will take incense and offer sacrifices to him.” As the count went with a large crowd and the saint, and as the martyr approached the temple, those beasts, unable to endure the martyr’s power and the glory that was upon him, made hissing noises and a commotion in the temple, so that the temple shook like an oak swaying in the wind. When the count and the crowds saw this, they fled. And the count said to the saint, “Do you see, old man, how great his power is? He allows no one to enter without incense.” The righteous man said, “Command your priest to open the temple, and I will go in.” Then the count commanded the priest to open it. But a certain other priest named Vitalis said, “I beg your illustrious authority: I cannot open it without incense and a sacrifice, for great is the wrath of the god Asclepius.” Then the priest took incense and offered it. And after opening the temple, he immediately ran away. Then the count said

to the righteous man, “Old man, if you dare and can enter the temple, then go in.” The saint approached, made the sign of Christ on his forehead, and entered the temple. And the beasts stood motionless. The saint prayed, saying, “Blessed are you, Lord God, who through your servant Daniel brought down the dragon and killed it. Likewise, Lord, now, in my presence, sinner that I am, put these beasts to death by your power and your divinity, so that your holy name may be glorified.” The beasts came out of the temple at the righteous man’s command and followed him, harming none of the people. When the crowds and the count saw the beasts come out of the temple, they ran away. Then the saint said to them, “Why are you running away? Do not be afraid. Stand still, and now you will see that they will die by the power of God.” Then the serpents began to speak with human voices: “Count, why did you bring into this city this righteous man to destroy us? You too will accomplish nothing.” When the count heard the beasts’ voices, he became afraid and wanted to flee. But the martyr said,

“Do not be afraid, sir, for they will die now.” Then the righteous man blew on them, and they fell before his feet and burst apart, so that everyone thought the crash was thunder. Then Saint Artemon said, “Do you see, sir, how your objects of worship have died by the power of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ?” The count was astonished that he had killed them without a staff or a weapon, for they were five cubits wide and twenty-five cubits long. When the chief priest saw this, he raised his voice and said, “Great is the God of the Christians, and great is the glory of this man, for by your power he has put these beasts to death.” He fell at the saint’s feet and said, “Servant of the living God, I beg you: I will not leave you. Mark me with the power of your God, so that I may become wholly a lamb of your flock. For until now I have been deceived, putting my trust in the pagan shrines and in these beasts.” When the crowd and the ruler had departed, the ruler, unable to bear the shame, ordered the saint to be brought to the judgment seat, so that he could question him before the crowd. When the martyr had been brought in, he said:

the count to him: “By the great goddess Artemis and the twelve-rayed sun, if you do not tell me by what power you killed these remarkable serpents, I will torture you in every limb.” Saint Artemon said, “By the power of Christ and of Raphael the archangel I killed these beasts.” The count said, “Can someone crucified by our people have any power?” Saint Artemon said, “You whose mind is darkened, you ancient serpent, you slave of the fiery abyss, do you still turn away, unwilling to hear that the beasts died by the power of God?” Then the count ordered an iron bed to be heated red-hot and the limbs to be cut from his body. And the count said to him, “Do you see, old man, how your flesh is now being consumed by fire?” But the righteous man looked up to heaven and said, “Lord Jesus Christ, do not forgive the impure count, since he has dared to do this to me. But see, Lord, that I am enduring this for your name’s sake. Grant me endurance, then, so that he may be utterly put to shame. Hear, O God, the prayers of your servant and my supplication, O Lord of hosts.

For you alone are God over all the kingdoms of the inhabited world. For you, Lord, made heaven and earth and everything wonderful beneath heaven. You are Lord of all, and there is no one who can resist you. Save me by your mercy, Lord. For you sanctified the image of your servant Abel, who was slain in his innocence, and guided your faithful servant Enoch to the heights, taking him up. You completed the ark and preserved righteous Noah. You exalted the priest Melchizedek with a blessing, and glorified Abraham, who was tested through sacrifices. You multiplied children from the seed of glorious Jacob. You snatched hospitable Lot from the burning fire. You blessed Job, who was strong in endurance. By your will, Joseph conquered the passions of the flesh through self-restraint. Through piety there grew mighty against his enemies your faithful servant Moses. Thus all who have been made righteous praise you, the God who glorified them. And I, Lord my God, your servant, pray to you: have mercy on me in your mercy, and help me by your power.” And while the righteous man was saying this, one of the [?]

that were in Laodicea, the bishop’s city, followed his trail and came to Caesarea. And coming into the midst of the crowd, it fell at the feet of the holy martyr and licked his feet. And standing before the count, it spoke with a human voice: “You filthy, wicked man, son of the devil, companion of fire, kinsman of darkness! Why do you torture Artemon, the servant of God, so cruelly? For behold, I am a wild animal who lived in the wilderness, but now I have been sent into the city by this man. Today it is two days since I left the bishop’s city, seeking and tracking my master. For I am compelled by the Holy Spirit to expose your evil thoughts. Know this, dignitary: Artemon, the servant of God, will be avenged. For two birds will throw you into a boiling cauldron, and all your flesh will boil away and turn to liquid, because you have tortured a righteous man and holy servant of Christ so cruelly.” And the count became angry at hearing a wild animal speak, and ordered his soldiers to pierce it. But it leaped far away

and went after the ruler’s table companion, and he immediately breathed his last. The count, distressed by what had happened, rose from the judgment seat and went into the praetorium. The next day he ordered a cauldron to be made, pitch to be put into it and heated, and Saint Artemon to be bound head downward and thrown into it, so that he might quickly be rid of him. The servants came and said to the count, “We have done as you ordered. The cauldron is boiling and spilling over.” But the count did not believe them and said, “Let us go and see the work, and then let the gray-haired old man be brought.” As the count sat in his chariot and approached the cauldron, suddenly two angels came from heaven in the form of eagles, seized the count from his chariot, and threw him into the cauldron. He boiled away completely, so that not even his bones could be found. The saint was praying with his knees bent, saying, “Lord, you are my refuge from the affliction that surrounds me. And it is you, Lord, who pulled my feet from the net of those hunting me.” When the soldiers and all the people saw what had happened, they fled, and

the saint remained alone in the place where he was. Then the saint knelt and prayed in that place, and a great quantity of water gushed up. Then Vitalius the priest came and said to the blessed martyr, “God’s judgment is righteous, for he will not allow his holy one to see decay.” Grant me too, master, the washing of incorruption, and pray for me that I may be delivered from my sins. And I will be his true servant. I will not turn away from you or from the knowledge of Christ. When Vitalius was about to be baptized, two men in white robes came down to the water and laid their hands on his head. And they enlightened him. Saint Artemon stood between them. As Vitalius came out of the water, the martyr gave him his hand. Vitalius sang, saying, “The Lord is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear?” That same night a voice came from heaven, saying, “Artemon, servant of the Most High and fellow partaker with Christ, leave this city and go to Asia, to the place called Vili, which is by the sea. For there you will find Alexander and his mother Pyrronia.

For they too have been sent there, and you too will cleanse many people of demons and of various afflictions. For it has been granted to you to be glorified there by people. For many there have been led astray, not knowing the glory of Christ.” When morning came, all those who had been baptized gathered together. The blessed man took bread and broke it, and filled a cup and gave it to them, saying, “This bread is the body of Christ.” And of the cup: “This is the blood poured out for our souls. Take care, children, that no one separates you from the love of Christ. Stand firm, for I have been commanded to go to Asia.” When Anatolius, bishop of the city of Caesarea, heard that many had been baptized by him and that he taught the true word, he left the church with a large crowd and went to the righteous Artemon to greet him with a kiss. Then the bishop prayed with the saint. They adorned the place where the martyr had suffered and built churches. He ordained many of those baptized by the martyr as priests and deacons, and appointed Vitalius as bishop. And he entrusted the regions of Palestine to him. He gave that place the name
